name: Volksgemeinschaft
summary: Volksgemeinschaft, the people's or national community, is the German idea of a nation united across classes, regions and denominations, with class conflict and party strife replaced by shared national purpose. Its dominant Nazi form defined membership by German blood and behaviour, put the people above the individual ("Gemeinnutz geht vor Eigennutz", "Du bist nichts, dein Volk ist alles"), demanded loyalty to the Fuehrer, and defined itself by excluding Jews and other "community aliens". Scholars stress that it was a promise and a practice of inclusion and exclusion, not a social reality.
scope: The idea named by the word, as the defining sources (USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia, Wildt's Docupedia entry, the German Historical Museum's LeMO entry) describe it: a classless, ethnically defined national community with duties before rights, which they present mainly in its Nazi form from the 1920s. They also say that monarchists, conservatives, liberals and socialists used the word, and that the Social Democrats and Landauer and Muehsam gave it other meanings; those usages are not profiled, and a statement is answered only where the defining sources tie the position to the concept. The 1920 NSDAP programme (points 4 to 6 and its common-good principle) and the national-community passages of Mein Kampf are used because the defining sources name the programme's point 4 and Mein Kampf's translator names the concept. Nazism's wider doctrine and the regime's other policies are not used.

class-collaboration.rationale: Hitler promised to restore social harmony by bringing white- and blue-collar workers together and ending class hatred and conflict, and the concept was set against class struggle.

workers-nation.rationale: Mein Kampf says the German worker must be brought back into the folk-community and rescued from the folly of internationalism, which clashes with nation and fatherland.

defeat-own-government-war.rationale: The community was to stand as a fate-bound whole in the Second World War, sworn to life and death, leaving no room for workers to work for their own government's defeat.

class-struggle-history.rationale: Mein Kampf, in its national-community points, calls the racial problem the key to understanding human history, which excludes class conflict as the main driving force.

ethnic-nation.rationale: The 1920 programme makes only people of German blood fellow countrymen, regardless of creed, and the national community was defined on race and ethnicity.

citizenship-by-descent.rationale: The Reich Citizenship Law of 1935 let only a person of German or related blood who served the people be a citizen, so citizenship followed descent.

racial-franchise.rationale: Under the regime, Jews, Black people and Roma and Sinti were barred from citizenship and disenfranchised as racially alien, leaving political rights to those of German or related blood.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Nazi laws legalized inequality and excluded whole groups from the national community, so rights before the law were not equal for all people.

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: The Nuremberg Laws prohibited relationships between Jews and non-Jews as race defilement, and the public was urged to report them to the police.

heritable-defect-limits.rationale: The law of 14 July 1933 permitted compulsory sterilisation and hereditary health courts ordered it in about 199,000 of 224,000 cases in three years; the disabled had no place in the community.

race-social-construct.rationale: The regime excluded Jews from the community by racial-biological criteria and applied them through persecution, treating race as a biological fact.

religious-nation.rationale: Membership was defined by German blood regardless of creed or religious denomination, not by a shared religion.

one-party-rule.rationale: The Nazis made abolishing the multiparty system an openly declared aim, calling parties the main obstacle to the Volksgemeinschaft, and set up the one-party state in 1933 with terror and bans.

suppress-opposition.rationale: After 30 January 1933 the regime used terror, newspaper bans, party-house seizures and the killing of officials against the KPD, SPD and later all other parties.

democracy-best.rationale: The Nazis blamed the multiparty system for "democratic chaos", abolished it in the name of the Volksgemeinschaft, and made party plurality and diversity of opinion an obstacle to be removed.

leader-cult.rationale: Nazi propaganda reinforced the idea that Hitler embodied the national will and staged mass events built on the Hitler myth to create the community.

strong-leader.rationale: The Fuehrerprinzip, the characteristic structural element of the Volksgemeinschaft, posited the unity of people and Fuehrer and demanded unconditional loyalty and obedience.

total-state.rationale: LeMO says the Nazi state aimed at complete shaping of public and private life, with other interests subordinate to the needs of the state and the Volksgemeinschaft.

state-harmful.rationale: The community was realised through a one-party state and totalitarian rule, so the state was strengthened, not abolished.

night-watchman-state.rationale: The regime used the state to coordinate society, persecute opponents and control membership of the community, far beyond protecting people from violence.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Its slogans were "Gemeinnutz geht vor Eigennutz" and "Du bist nichts, dein Volk ist alles", and personal freedom rights were not to exist beside the community's needs.

individual-rights-only.rationale: Wildt writes that Volksgenossen were not citizens with guaranteed liberties and the concept was not about equality of individuals; LeMO adds that personal freedom rights were not to exist.

self-interest-moral.rationale: The slogan "Gemeinnutz geht vor Eigennutz" ranks the common good above self-interest, which it does not treat as a moral good.

person-over-state.rationale: The core sentence of the regime, "Du bist nichts, dein Volk ist alles", treats the individual as a servant of the people.

single-common-good.rationale: The concept was invoked against class struggle and party bickering, urging unity of the whole nation over competing groups, though not a "reasoned" common good in the statement's sense.

political-violence-never.rationale: Violence was shared among Volksgenossen and used to draw a sharp line between the community and its "enemies of the people", as in the boycotts and race-defilement parades.

boycott-minority-shops.rationale: Boycotts of Jewish shops went on well beyond 1 April 1933, and Germans who kept shopping at Jewish stores were denounced as traitors to the people.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: Under the regime that promoted the national community, strikes were banned and factory discipline increased.

collective-bargaining.rationale: The regime froze wages at 1932 levels and banned strikes, so wages were not set by union negotiation.

independent-unions.rationale: The free trade unions were broken up on 2 May 1933, a day after the Nazis staged the Volksgemeinschaft at the May Day rallies.

legal-duty-to-work.rationale: Protective custody was extended to the "work-shy" and a 1937 decree let police imprison some 100,000 "asocial" people, among them the work-shy, for anti-community behaviour.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: Criminal police were freed from the limits of law and statute to create a community without criminals, and tax law was to be read by Nazi worldview.

criminalize-homosexuality.rationale: In 1935 the Nazis sharply tightened the penal provisions on sex between men, adding paragraph 175a, while reasoning about the Volksgemeinschaft led them not to extend them to women.

territorial-expansion.rationale: In occupied western Poland, territory was to be Germanised and the future German community defined by who was allowed to belong.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: Mein Kampf calls a healthy peasant class the basis of the national community and blames present evils on the imbalance between town and country.

democracy-needs-political-clash.rationale: The Nazis held that parties and the diversity of political opinion they spread were a main obstacle to the Volksgemeinschaft, and removed them.

traditional-family.rationale: Propaganda glorified farmers and soldiers as the basis of the Volksgemeinschaft and held the traditional, many-children family to be its germ cell and guarantor of moral order.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: Mother schools and the Mother's Cross assigned women a particular role in the Volksgemeinschaft as "serving motherhood", though the sources describe policy and organisations, not law.

uniformed-youth.rationale: The regime used the Hitler Youth to train youth for the community ideals of Volksgemeinschaft, readiness to sacrifice and military preparedness.

patriotic-education.rationale: Propaganda demanded that youth be educated to the Volksgemeinschaft, readiness to sacrifice and military preparedness, which is a national education though not framed as flag-and-anthem patriotism.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: The Nazis justified expropriating Jews by treating all property as "Volksvermoegen" serving the Volksgemeinschaft.

property-fundamental.rationale: Jewish property was confiscated once the Nuremberg Laws placed Jews outside the Volksgemeinschaft, so property rights were easily overridden.

welfare-for-citizens.rationale: Party welfare served the racially defined Volksgemeinschaft and gave Jews, the "asocial" and others no help, which fits reserving benefits for members.

encourage-eccentricity.rationale: Protective custody was extended to Bible Students, the "work-shy" and the "asocial", as the system sought to remake the Volksgemeinschaft and exclude the socially undesirable.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Mother schools taught care of folk culture and customs, with folk songs and tales meant to convey the Volksgemeinschaft idea.

party-controls-media.rationale: The Propaganda Ministry, set up in March 1933, took complete control of cultural life and the media, and the press was brought into line to serve Nazi worldview.

left-right-obsolete.rationale: The Nazis offered the Volksgemeinschaft as the solution to all the political and social oppositions of the Weimar Republic.

notes: Themes searched in the saved sources: class relations, citizenship and race, the individual and the common good, leadership, parties and elections, unions and strikes, welfare and work, religion, family, war and expansion, economy and property, immigration. The defining sources describe the concept and the regime's practice; they say little on most economic, ecological, technological and foreign-policy statements, and Nazism's wider doctrine was not used as a coatrack, so most answers are null. Where the regime's practice settles a statement (laws, banned strikes, persecution) the answer rests on the record.
